panels.rationale: Axial head CT of a real infant patient showing a large right subgaleal hematoma and a small epidural hematoma (arrowed). The caption explicitly attributes this disproportionate hemorrhage after a 50 cm fall to subsequently confirmed type 1 von Willebrand disease, and the article title frames the case as abuse versus bleeding disorder. The hemorrhage is the clinical manifestation of vWD (soft-tissue/subcutaneous hematoma after minor trauma) supported by panel-specific caption evidence. Subgaleal hemorrhage beyond the neonatal period is described as highly atypical, hence typicality atypical. Skin tone not assessable on CT; age group child per caption description of the infant. [raw subtype: type 1]

panels.figure_caption: Head computed tomography demonstrating epidural and subgaleal hematomas. Head computed tomography confirmed a large right subgaleal hematoma and a small epidural hematoma (arrow). In infants beyond the newborn period, subgaleal hemorrhage is uncommon. Prior to this incident, the patient had no history of excessive mucocutaneous bleeding (such as easy bruising or prolonged bleeding after vaccinations), and there was no known family history of bleeding disorders. According to the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network criteria [1], a fall from less than 0.9 m in infants is considered a non-severe mechanism of injury. Therefore, the development of a large subgaleal and epidural hematoma following a 50 cm fall is highly atypical. Such a hemorrhage, disproportionate to the reported causal trauma, should raise concern for possible child abuse. To thoroughly evaluate the possibility of non-accidental injury, a multidisciplinary child protection assessment was conducted. The injury mechanism described by the caregivers was consistent, and no additional unexplained bruising was noted. Furthermore, skeletal survey and fundoscopic examination were unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL), while platelet count, platelet function closure time, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time were within normal ranges. Initial coagulation studies showed elevated von Willebrand factor (vWF) activity (198.5%; reference range, 58.0–172.0%). However, repeat testing two months later revealed markedly reduced vWF antigen (23.6%; reference range, 55.9–161.6%) and vWF activity (24.6%), suggestive of type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD). Further longitudinal follow-up and repeat testing are warranted. Subgaleal hemorrhage is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition in which blood accumulates between the skull periosteum and the galea aponeurotica. Because the subgaleal space is not limited by cranial sutures, it can rapidly accommodate a massive amount of blood [2], explaining our patient’s marked hemoglobin drop to 7.3 g/dL. While it is most commonly a neonatal emergency associated with assisted vaginal delivery, beyond the neonatal period, even minor mechanical trauma can trigger significant subgaleal hemorrhage in the presence of underlying coagulopathies [2]. Among these, vWD is the most commonly inherited bleeding disorder. While it may present with such disproportionate or unexpected bleeding in clinical practice [3,4], vWD can be underdiagnosed in young children who have not yet experienced hemostatic challenges, typically manifesting as excessive bleeding following surgery or traumatic injury [5]. Furthermore, everyday circumstances that may prompt clinical evaluation during childhood include recurrent mucocutaneous bleeding, such as frequent epistaxis, extensive bruising, or prolonged bleeding from minor wounds [3,5]. However, because mild bruising and nosebleeds are also commonly observed in healthy developing children, early detection of vWD can be particularly difficult and requires careful clinical suspicion [5]. In addition, acutely establishing a vWD diagnosis can be challenging. vWF levels and activity vary substantially due to both non-genetic and genetic factors. Non-genetic factors such as acute physiological stress and inflammation following trauma can transiently elevate vWF levels, potentially masking underlying vWD [3]. Furthermore, the ABO blood group is a major genetic modifier, accounting for up to 30% of plasma vWF variability; individuals with blood type O naturally have approximately 25% lower baseline vWF levels [6]. Given that our patient has blood type B, her markedly reduced vWF levels (23.6%) during follow-up under non-stress conditions cannot be attributed to the effect of blood type O. Moreover, unlike platelet reactivity, which is physiologically decreased in neonates, plasma vWF levels are typically high in early infancy [7]; therefore, developmental immaturity was effectively ruled out as a cause for her markedly low levels. Taken together, these findings significantly strengthen the clinical suspicion of underlying vWD. Specific genetic testing was not performed, as it is currently not a part of standard initial evaluations given the complexity of the VWF gene. Furthermore, although there was no known family history of bleeding disorders in the present case, it should be noted that a negative family history does not rule out the diagnosis. Type 1 vWD frequently exhibits incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, and de novo variants [3]. Consistent with our findings, the recent literature emphasizes that non-neonatal subgaleal hemorrhage is exceedingly rare and can signal an unrecognized coagulopathy or recurrent injury when it occurs after minor trauma [8]. For instance, a recently described closely analogous case involved a young child who developed a massive subgaleal hematoma following a similar 50 cm fall, which ultimately unmasked a combined bleeding disorder involving VWF deficiency [9]. This case highlights that disproportionate hemorrhage after seemingly minor trauma should prompt evaluation for both non-accidental injury and occult bleeding disorders. Moreover, it illustrates that initial vWF levels can be highly variable, and repeat testing is essential to confirm an underlying bleeding diathesis.

plate_findings.evidence: Multiple ecchymoses were observed following chiropractic manipulation. (A) Dorsum of the right forearm

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of the dorsum of the right forearm showing a large ecchymosis in a patient with von Willebrand disease; ecchymoses are a classic mucocutaneous bleeding manifestation of VWD. B: Clinical photograph of the ventral right forearm with a large elongated ecchymosis in a von Willebrand disease patient; classic bruising manifestation. C: Clinical photograph of the sacral area showing a large ecchymosis in a patient with von Willebrand disease, consistent with disease-related bruising after minor trauma/manipulation.

panels.rationale: Coronal CT reconstruction of a real patient with type III von Willebrand disease showing a large (≈700 cc) heterogeneous left iliopsoas muscle hematoma, indicated by a red arrow. The article title and in-text mentions explicitly attribute the hematoma to von Willebrand disease, making this a disease-specific manifestation (soft-tissue bleeding/haematoma) rather than a comparison or control image. [raw subtype: type_III]

CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: The first CT coronal reconstruction shows a heterogeneous image in the left iliopsoas muscle, consistent with a hematoma, with an estimated volume of 700 cc.
in_text_mentions: Following a chiropractic consultation, the patient presented with a large left inguinal hematoma, femoral neuropathy, and pain 10/10 on the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS). A CT scan revealed a 689 cc (Figure 1) hematoma in the left iliopsoas muscle. She was admitted, and an interdisciplinary consultation with hematology confirmed a diagnosis of type III vWD. Given the lack of recombinant factor VIII at our hospital, initial treatment included transnasal desmopressin, tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitates, and fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) to stabilize her hemoglobin levels.

The dose was calculated on the basis of factor VIII coagulation. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Surgical clinical photo of a child with von Willebrand disease showing a left gingivo-labial submucosal swelling/mass, consistent with a bleeding-related pseudotumor/haematoma; article title ties the lesion to von Willebrand disease, but the manifestation is atypical and the exact vocabulary match is imperfect. B: Intraoral surgical clinical photo showing a large collection of coagulated blood in a child with von Willebrand disease; this supports oral mucosal bleeding in the setting of the disease, though the image is an atypical/lesional presentation.

panels.figure_caption: Biopsy. Submucosal plane with increased volume in the left gingivo-labial region (surgical image A). Large collection of coagulated blood (surgical image B)
in_text_mentions: ombin time of 12.1 seconds, partial thromboplastin time of 34.0 seconds, as well as a normal platelet count. A biopsy was done of clot fragments removed from the left maxillary sinus cavity and also of the tumor (Figure 2) due to the possible differential diagnosis of an expansive malignant process, which revealed irregular tissue fragments named as “left maxillary tumor” of 3 x 2.5 x 0.5 centimeters, covered by areas of fibroblast proliferation and dense connective tissue similar to a scar. Histopathologically, areas of proliferating fibroblasts and dense fibrous connective tissue were found.
